cases.title: [BUG] AI chat: text typed in the message box is wiped when the assistant replies
cases.notes:
**Fix the AI chat so text typed in the composer is never cleared by an incoming assistant reply. Urgent.**

## Problem

Valentin reports a huge bug: "There's a huge bug in the AI chat whereby my message in the text box gets wiped whenever you reply." A user types in the composer while the assistant is working, or before sending. When the reply arrives or streams in, the typed text disappears and the user loses what they were writing.

## Current behavior

-   Open the AI chat and send a message so the assistant starts working.
    
-   Type a new message in the composer, without sending it.
    
-   The reply arrives or streams in. The composer is empty.
    

## Expected behavior

Text typed in the composer stays until the user **sends it, clears it or switches chat sessions**. An incoming reply never touches it.

## Requirements

-   Do not clear the draft when a turn **finishes, fails or is stopped**.
    
-   Keep draft text **per chat session**, so it survives streaming updates, switching chats and reloads.
    
-   Cover both the **docked sidebar chat** and the **full-screen /chat** view.
    
-   Keep queued-message and focus behavior unchanged (see Related).
    

## Cause to investigate

Engineering to check each of these, then fix the one that applies:

-   The composer value is reset on reply-complete or stream-finish.
    
-   The message list re-renders or changes key, which remounts the composer.
    
-   Session state hydration overwrites the composer value.
    
-   Draft text sits in view-level state instead of a store keyed by session id.
    

## Done when

-   Typing while a reply streams in leaves the text intact, in the docked chat and in /chat.
    
-   The text survives turn finish, failure and stop.
    
-   The draft returns after switching to another chat and back, and after a reload.
    
-   A test fails if a reply-complete event clears the composer.
    

## Related

-   [HTPR-7674](https://app.hypertask.ai/detail/project-15/7674), related. An inbox reply typed right after opening can be wiped before sending.
    
-   [HTPR-7767](https://app.hypertask.ai/detail/project-15/7767), related. Queued messages are lost when switching chats and back.
    
-   [HTPR-7762](https://app.hypertask.ai/detail/project-15/7762), related. Full-screen new session does not focus the chat box.
    
-   [HTPR-6038](https://app.hypertask.ai/detail/project-15/6038), builds on. Queue messages while the agent works (the queue feature ticket).

cases.title: Speed up task creation from the AI chat
cases.notes:
Cut the time from brief to created ticket when the sidebar AI chat creates a task, by measuring each stage first and then removing avoidable work.

## Problem

Valentin reports that task creation from the AI chat takes **very long**. No timing data has been gathered yet, so the slow stage is unknown.

## Hypothesis

If we time each stage and remove extra model round trips and oversized prompt and board context, then AI-chat task creation gets faster. This is an estimate until the stage timings are in.

## Requirements

-   **Measure first.** Log the duration of each stage from the user's brief to the created ticket: chat model turn, context loading, task writer call, task save, and UI update.
    
-   **Remove avoidable model round trips.** Count the model calls per create. Drop or merge any that do not change the result.
    
-   **Shrink the payload.** Reduce the prompt and the board context sent to the model. Keep what the writer needs for board format, labels and columns.
    
-   **Set a latency budget.** Proposed: take the target from the measured baseline and Ctrl+J, and write it in a comment. Do not pick a number before the baseline exists.
    
-   **Keep output unchanged.** The chat keeps using the same task writer path as Ctrl+J, CLI and MCP (HTPR-7363). Title, description, priority and size must not change.
    
-   **Scope.** This is the engine side only. The interaction and UI improvement is a separate ticket.
    

## Acceptance criteria

-   A baseline of per-stage timings from real chat creates is posted in a comment, with sample count.
    
-   The slowest stage is named, and the fix targets it.
    
-   A before and after comparison on the same briefs shows the latency change against the agreed budget.
    
-   Output structure and style match Ctrl+J for the same brief.
    

## Suggested metrics

-   Time from send to created ticket, p50, p75 and p95, as in HTPR-5596.
    
-   Number of model calls per task creation.
    
-   Prompt input tokens per creation.
    
-   Task creation error rate, which must not rise.
    

## ICE assessment (estimated)

-   Impact 7: slow creation hits a frequent chat action.
    
-   Confidence 6: cause unmeasured so far.
    
-   Ease 6: depends on which stage dominates.
    
-   Total 19/30.
    

## Related

-   Builds on [HTPR-7363](https://app.hypertask.ai/detail/project-15/7363): chat creates tasks with the same task writer as Ctrl+J.
    
-   Builds on [HTPR-5756](https://app.hypertask.ai/detail/project-15/5756): reduce task-creation latency below 1.5s p75.
    
-   Builds on [HTPR-5596](https://app.hypertask.ai/detail/project-15/5596): publish the collected task-creation latency in the speed report.
cases.reference:
Problem

Task creation from the sidebar AI chat takes very long. Valentin, 2026-10-24: "I find task creation takes VERY long when done from the ai chat."

No chat-specific timing exists, so the slow stage is unknown. The one measured number on this board is for the manual save path, not the chat: desktop p50 1,155 ms, p75 2,054 ms, p95 2,516 ms over 30 samples (Aug 22 to 29 window, Reduce production task-creation latency below 1.5s p75). The chat adds at least one model turn on top of that path.

Hypothesis

Chat creation pays for stages that add nothing visible: a chat model turn before the writer runs, board context loaded fresh per call, an oversized prompt, and possibly a separate title call. Trimming those should cut the wait without changing output.

What to do

  1. Measure first. Log per-stage duration from send to created ticket: context load, chat turn, task-writer call, title generation, save, UI update. Post the baseline with sample count in a comment.

  2. Count the model calls per single task creation, and remove or merge any that do not change the result.

  3. Shrink the payload. Cut prompt and board context to what the writer needs: board format, labels, columns. Cache context across turns in one chat.

  4. Set the budget from data. Proposed: the chat path lands within the Ctrl+J p95 for the same brief, since it should be the same writer (AI chat creates tasks with the same task writer as Ctrl+J, CLI and MCP). Confirm the number after the baseline, not before.

Acceptance

  • Per-stage baseline posted, with the slowest stage named and the fix aimed at it.

  • Before and after on the same set of briefs, against the agreed budget.

  • Model calls per creation and prompt input tokens both go down, or the ticket explains why they cannot.

  • Error rate does not rise. A failed title step must not silently retry, see vercel: [ai/chat/stream] title generation failed.

  • Output structure and style still match Ctrl+J for the same brief.

  • Latency reporting follows the rules in Speed report: publish authenticated task-creation latency already collected: p50, p75, p95, error rate, sample count, at least 20 samples.

Scope

Engine and pipeline only. The visible interaction change (ticket first, body after) is AI chat: show the created ticket fast and fill in the body behind it.

ICE (estimated, pre-baseline)

Impact 7, Confidence 6, Ease 6 = 19/30. Confidence is held back until the stage timings exist.

What the numbers mean:

-   sol medium used almost the same tokens as sol high on this task. The saving there is only wall time. luna used one extra turn but its estimated price is about 15x lower.
    
-   The price column is hax's estimate at API list prices. Under the subscription, nobody yet knows how much of the weekly % a luna token costs vs a sol token. That is the main thing this trial measures.
    
-   One sol medium run hung on its first model call for 600 s until timeout (1 of 10 runs overall). Probably a stream stall, not the model. Runners need a stall watchdog (kill and retry after about 3 min with no output).
    
-   A tiny task can't show quality on real tickets. The redo rate below covers that.
    

## Trial setting

-   Cheap arm: **gpt-6-luna, effort high** (passed 3/3). Fallback if luna's redo rate is bad: gpt-6.1-sol medium.
    
-   Normal arm: gpt-6.1-sol high, unchanged.
    
-   Review stays on gpt-6-astra / Opus. Fast mode stays off everywhere.
    

## Routing rule (at ticket start only)

-   Cheap arm if the ticket has label `easy` or `intensity:easy`, OR it is small and well specified: one file area and a clear done-when.
    
-   Everything else stays on sol high.
    
-   Picked when a runner starts a ticket. Never change a live ticket or a running session.
    
-   Log the arm on the ticket (one line: arm, model, effort) so the numbers can be split later.

cases.title: Shrink starting rules files
cases.notes:
## Why

Every fresh session pays for always-loaded rules before its first prompt. Measured on hypertask-vps, 25 Oct 2026, in ~/projects/hypertask, "say ok", no router, fast mode off:

-   Claude Code (haiku, `claude -p --output-format json`): **35,318** input tokens. Bare baseline with no settings, skills or MCP: 21,012.
    
-   Codex (`codex exec --json`): **28,259** tokens per model call. "say ok" cost **55,663**, because a global rule makes Codex `cat` the unslop skill (6.6 KB) before replying.
    
-   hax (`--no-session -p`): about **12k**.
    

Biggest always-loaded rule files:

-   Repo `AGENTS.md`: 21,667 bytes, about 5.4k tokens, loaded by Codex and hax. Claude does not auto-load it; repo `CLAUDE.md` (2,584 bytes) already points into its sections.
    
-   `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`: 4,924 bytes, about 1.2k tokens.
    
-   `~/.codex/AGENTS.md`: 1,354 bytes, a separate Codex copy of global rules.
    

## What to do

1.  Make repo `AGENTS.md` the one source and keep it under about 5 KB: a short map ("read X when Y") that points to skills and `.claude/reference/`.
    
2.  Move each current `AGENTS.md` section (Claude Code and Codex sessions, CLI and MCP repositories, Hypertask Ticket Access, Ticket comments, Claim a ticket, Repository Workflow, CI contract, Reuse existing UI, Stack Orientation, AI models, Feature flags) into an existing or new skill or reference file. Where a rule is a check, move it into code or a hook instead of prose.
    
3.  Make `CLAUDE.md` point at `AGENTS.md` (or import it) so Claude and Codex read the same map. No second copy.
    
4.  Delete the duplicate Codex copy (`~/.codex/AGENTS.md`): fold its credential-safety and ticket-writing rules into the global map or the matching skill.
    
5.  Stop the global rule that makes Codex read the unslop skill before every reply. Load it only when writing prose for Valentin.
    
6.  Nothing lost: the PR description lists every section and the file it moved to.
    

## Done when

-   Always-loaded rules are under about 5 KB per harness.
    
-   Measured before/after with the same commands as above: Codex per-call startup drops by at least 4k tokens (28,259 to 24k or less), the "say ok" run no longer reads a skill (no second model call), and Claude repo startup does not grow (35,318 or less).
    
-   One `/ship` ticket still runs end to end on the new map.

`CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` are protected. Open the PR, send its link to HT Product Lead (`session-say hypertasks-10`) and add a comment on this ticket naming HT Product Lead. HT Product Lead reviews and merges.

cases.title: Ctrl+K: archive every ticket in a column in one action
cases.notes:
Valentin, 2026-10-25: "ctrl+k archive all tickets in column feature pls so i can easily archive a whole coluimns ticket pls"

## What he wants

A way to archive a whole column at once. From Ctrl+K, he picks a column, for example Feature, and every ticket in it is archived in one action, instead of archiving tickets one by one.

## What this thread settled

-   The entry point is the Ctrl+K command menu, because that is where he already drives the board.
    
-   The action takes a column, not the whole board, so one column can be cleared without touching the others.
    
-   Archiving removes the tickets from the board the way single-ticket archive already does; it does not delete anything permanent.
    
-   Single-ticket archive keeps working exactly as it does now.
    

## The deeper pass

A destructive bulk action is only safe if it is hard to trigger by accident and easy to undo. Before it runs, show the column name and the exact ticket count and ask for one confirmation. After it runs, show a result line with the count and a single undo for that action, because a wrong column will otherwise cost him the tickets he meant to keep.

Start from the real paths, not a guess: the existing single-ticket archive action and its permission check, the command menu's existing column commands, and the board's archive view so the result can be seen. Method: reuse the current archive call in a loop over the column's tickets, batch it, and report tickets that refused individually rather than failing the whole run.

Outside proof: on a test board with at least one ticket in two different columns, archive one column from Ctrl+K, then show the column is empty, the other column is untouched, the tickets appear in the board archive, and undo returns them all. Repeat on phone.

## Done when

-   Ctrl+K offers archiving one column, naming the column.
    
-   It asks for confirmation with the ticket count before archiving.
    
-   After archiving, the column is empty, the other columns are unchanged, and the tickets are in the board archive.
    
-   One undo restores the tickets from that action.
    
-   Works on desktop and phone.

HT Product Lead Ticket for review. Valentin's plan, 2026-10-25: runners orchestrate on cheap tokens, hax does the leg work, hooks enforce it (not rules text), 10 hax runners on standby, and any session can switch between Claude, Codex and Grok with one command.

-   **Runners do the code work themselves.** Runners are Claude Code on DeepSeek (deepseek-flash through Claude Code Router). They should only orchestrate and start hax (Codex) helpers. Nothing enforces that. Today RUNNER 5 (tmux hypertask-2) made 95 Edit/Write calls and started 6 hax runs. RUNNER 3 (hypertask-8) made 63 Edit/Write calls and started no hax runs.
    
-   **DeepSeek is nearly empty.** Spend was $34.45 in about 2 days: about $22 today, 46,875 calls and 6.3B tokens. The balance is $5.48 and the low-balance alert is off. At zero every runner stops.
    
-   **No switchover.** There's no command to move a session, or the whole fleet, to another provider. Each harness loads skills, hooks and rules differently, so a session can't simply be restarted on another one.
    

### 2\. Who it affects

Valentin (spend, and the fleet stalls when a provider runs out). All runners (hypertask, hypertask-2 to 9, hypertasks-10, ceo-runner-1 to 8). Leads (HT Product Lead, Poteto Advisor). Every ticket in /ship.

### 3\. Recommendation: what poteto would do

Small PRs, one per part, in this order. Each part works on its own.

1.  **Leg-work hook (urgent, ship first).** A PreToolUse hook that applies to runner sessions only.
